## Boeing 2023 Form 10-K — Union Representation of Workforce (as of December 31, 2023)

Boeing reports a total workforce of approximately **171,000** employees (14% located outside the U.S.) as of December 31, 2023, of which approximately **57,000** were union members.

### Overall union representation
- **33%** of Boeing's total workforce was union represented as of December 31, 2023 (approximately 57,000 employees under collective bargaining agreements). This figure appears in the Risk Factors section ("Some of our and our suppliers' workforces are represented by labor unions, which may lead to work stoppages," p. 9 of the 10-K). Boeing also notes its union relationships span **10 U.S. labor organizations and 4 non-U.S. labor organizations**.

### By union (Item 1, "Human Capital," p. 2 of the 10-K)

| Union | Percent of employees represented | Major agreement status |
|---|---|---|
| International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM) | **21%** | Two major agreements: IAM District 751 (Washington) expiring September 2024; IAM District 837 (Missouri) expiring July 2025 |
| Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace (SPEEA) | **10%** | Two major agreements (SPEEA Professional and SPEEA Technical), both expiring October 2026 |
| United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (UAW) | **1%** | One major agreement with UAW District 1069 (Pennsylvania) expiring April 2027 |

Note: the three union percentages (21% + 10% + 1% = 32%) are rounded and reflect the principal unions; the filing's overall figure for the union-represented share of the total workforce is 33%.

## Boeing 2025 Form 10-K (BA_2025_10K.pdf) — IAM District 837

**Note on sourcing:** these figures appear in two places in the filing — Item 1 (Human Capital, p.4) and Item 1A Risk Factors (p.11) for the strike; MD&A Overview (p.26) for the calendar dates; and the Item 1 collective-bargaining table (p.4) for the contract.

### 1. The 2025 strike by IAM District 837

| Item | What the filing says | What it refers to |
|---|---|---|
| Employee count | Approximately **3,200 employees** | The number of Boeing employees *represented by* IAM District 837 (at Boeing's St. Louis area sites) — not a count of individuals who actually participated in the walkout |
| Duration | **101 days** | The length of the work stoppage ("went out on strike for 101 days") |
| Start date | **August 4, 2025** | Date the work stoppage was initiated |
| End date | **November 13, 2025** | Date District 837 members voted to ratify a new contract, "thereby ending the work stoppage initiated on August 4, 2025" |

**Operational effect as described:** the strike "disrupted our St. Louis operations and impacting programs including F/A-18, F-15, T-7A, MQ-25 and Weapons."

**Notable context the filing provides:** the strike occurred "despite having in each case reached a tentative agreement with union leadership on the terms of the proposed contract and union leadership having recommended its members vote to ratify the proposed contract." (The filing makes the same point about the 2024 IAM District 751 strike, which lasted 53 days, began September 13, 2024, and ended with a ratification vote on November 4, 2024.)

### 2. Boeing's current CBA with IAM District 837

| Item | What the filing says | What it refers to |
|---|---|---|
| Principal location | **Missouri** | Location of the agreement in the Item 1 table of principal collective bargaining agreements |
| Expiration date | **July 2030** | Expiration of the current (successor) agreement with District 837 |

Other relevant table context: IAM collectively accounts for **25% of Boeing's total workforce**; District 837 is one of Boeing's three IAM agreements, the others being District 70 (Kansas, expires June 2027) and District 751 (Washington, expires September 2028). The filing does not state an explicit start date or term length for the District 837 contract — only the July 2030 expiration (implying a term running from the November 2025 ratification to mid-2030).

### Workforce context in the same filing (as of December 31, 2025)
- Total workforce: approximately **182,000**, with 14% located outside the U.S.
- Approximately **72,000 union members**, or about **40%** of the total workforce
- **32 independent agreements** with nine unions in the U.S., plus agreements with **18 employee representative bodies** internationally
- SPEEA represents approximately 16,000 employees, with two contracts expiring in **October 2026**

Based on Apple's fiscal 2024 Form 10-K (AAPL_2024_10K.pdf), the MD&A attributes four fiscal 2024 results being unfavorably affected by weak foreign currencies versus the U.S. dollar:

**Segment net sales (Item 7, p. 22 of the 10-K / PDF p. 25)**

1. **Greater China net sales** — $66,952M, down 8% from $72,559M. The 10-K states: "The weakness in the **renminbi** relative to the U.S. dollar had an unfavorable year-over-year impact on Greater China net sales during 2024." (Segment net sales declined primarily due to lower iPhone and iPad sales, with currency an additional headwind.)

2. **Japan net sales** — $25,052M, up 3% from $24,257M. "The weakness in the **yen** relative to the U.S. dollar had an unfavorable year-over-year impact on Japan net sales during 2024." (The increase itself was driven by higher iPhone net sales, which more than offset the currency drag.)

3. **Rest of Asia Pacific net sales** — $30,658M, up 4% from $29,615M. "The weakness in **foreign currencies** relative to the U.S. dollar had a **net** unfavorable year-over-year impact on Rest of Asia Pacific net sales during 2024." (Segment increase was primarily due to higher Services net sales.)

**Gross margin (Item 7, p. 24 of the 10-K / PDF p. 27)**

4. **Products gross margin and Products gross margin percentage** — $109,633M and 37.2%, up from $108,803M and 36.5%. "Products gross margin and Products gross margin percentage increased during 2024 compared to 2023 due to cost savings, partially offset by a different Products mix and **the weakness in foreign currencies relative to the U.S. dollar**." Here currency was a partial offset to an otherwise favorable result.

**Items not attributed to currency weakness**
- Americas and Europe net sales increases (no currency effect cited).
- Services gross margin/percentage (increase attributed to higher Services net sales and Services mix).
- R&D, SG&A, and the effective tax rate (tax rate driven by the $10.2B State Aid Decision charge, state taxes, foreign earnings rate, R&D credit, and share-based compensation).

**Supporting context**
- Item 7A (PDF p. 30) states generally that "a strengthening of the U.S. dollar will negatively affect the Company's net sales and gross margins as expressed in U.S. dollars," and reports a one-day 95%-confidence VAR loss on foreign currency derivatives of $538M in 2024 vs. $669M in 2023.
- Risk Factors (PDF p. 19) note that the weakening of foreign currencies adversely affects the U.S. dollar value of foreign currency–denominated sales and earnings, and that gross margins on foreign products have in the past been adversely affected by FX fluctuations.
- Note 4 (PDF pp. 40–41) discloses the FX hedging framework and derivative notionals (FX contracts designated as accounting hedges: $64,069M in 2024 vs. $74,730M in 2023; undesignated: $91,493M vs. $104,777M).

One nuance: the Consolidated Statements of Comprehensive Income show a positive foreign currency translation adjustment of $395M in 2024 (vs. a $765M loss in 2023), but the 10-K does not attribute this to currency weakness, and it is not one of the results described as unfavorably affected.

I found the relevant disclosures in Walmart's fiscal 2022 Form 10-K (year ended January 31, 2022). The filing gives pickup/delivery location counts at three levels.

## 1. Consolidated / company-wide (Item 1, "The Development of Our Company," p. 6)

> "In 2007, leveraging our physical stores, walmart.com launched its Site to Store service... To date, we now have **over 8,000 pickup and 6,000 delivery locations globally**."

- Covers: the entire company (Walmart U.S., Walmart International, and Sam's Club combined), i.e., all pickup and delivery locations globally.
- Qualifiers: "over" applies to the 8,000 pickup locations; the 6,000 delivery locations is stated without a qualifier.

## 2. Walmart U.S. segment (Item 1, "Omni-channel," p. 7)

> "As of January 31, 2022, we had **approximately 4,600 pickup locations and more than 3,500 same-day delivery locations**."

- Covers: the Walmart U.S. segment only (U.S., all 50 states, Washington D.C., Puerto Rico; "Walmart" and "Walmart Neighborhood Market" brands plus walmart.com), in the omni-channel discussion covering pickup and delivery, ship-from-store, and digital pharmacy fulfillment.
- Qualifiers: "approximately" for pickup; "more than" for same-day delivery.

## 3. Walmart International segment (Item 1, p. 9)

> "As of January 31, 2022, Walmart International had **approximately 2,900 pickup and over 1,900 delivery locations**."

- Covers: the Walmart International segment (23 countries as of January 2022) — pickup and delivery services in most of its markets, discussed in connection with same-day delivery in Mexico, the JD.com/JD Daojia partnerships in China, and Flipkart/PhonePe in India.
- Qualifiers: "approximately" for pickup; "over" for delivery.

## Notes on scope and related counts

- Sam's Club: the segment discussion does not state a pickup or delivery location count. It says Curbside Pickup is available at all clubs and refers to "delivery-from-club" (600 clubs at period end).
- These counts are distinct from the facility counts elsewhere in Item 1, which you excluded: 157 Walmart U.S. distribution facilities, 31 dedicated eCommerce fulfillment centers, 179 international distribution facilities, 83 dedicated international eCommerce fulfillment centers, more than 3,400 international eCommerce sort centers and last-mile delivery facilities in India, 28 Sam's Club distribution facilities, and 12 Sam's Club dedicated eCommerce fulfillment centers. Item 1 also separately notes Walmart U.S. can "ship or deliver directly from more than 3,500 stores" and international eCommerce shipments come from "more than 3,400 eCommerce sort centers and last-mile delivery facilities in India."
- The segment figures do not sum to the global "over 8,000 / 6,000" figures, consistent with the global number also reflecting Sam's Club locations; the filing does not reconcile the two.

## NVIDIA FY2024 Form 10-K — Inventory Provisions and Purchase-Obligation Charges in Cost of Revenue

Source document: `NVDA_2024_10K.pdf` (fiscal year ended January 28, 2024). The filing discloses these amounts in two places that must be read together: the MD&A "Gross Profit and Gross Margin" discussion (p.40) and the footnotes to Note 10, "Balance Sheet Components" (pp.68, 70).

### Fiscal 2024 amounts

| Amount (FY2024) | Where disclosed | What it represents |
|---|---|---|
| **$2.2 billion** (total) | MD&A, "Gross Profit and Gross Margin," p.40 | "Provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations totaled $2.2 billion" for fiscal 2024 — the combined gross charges to cost of revenue covering both on-hand inventory write-downs and excess purchase obligations |
| **$774 million** | Note 10, footnote (1) to Inventories, p.68 | Inventory provision recorded in cost of revenue — write-down of inventory to the lower of cost or net realizable value for excess or obsolete quantities of products/components (raw materials, work-in-process, finished goods) |
| **~$1.4 billion** ("approximately") | Note 10, footnote (1) to Excess inventory purchase obligations, p.70 | Expense recorded in cost of revenue for "inventory purchase obligations in excess of our current demand projections, supplier charges and for penalties related to cancellations and underutilization" — i.e., non-cancellable supplier commitments beyond forecast demand, plus cancellation/underutilization penalties |
| **$540 million** (release) | MD&A, "Gross Profit and Gross Margin," p.40 | Provision release: "Sales of previously reserved inventory or settlements of excess inventory purchase obligations" — a credit to cost of revenue |

### Cross-check and net effect

- The two Note 10 components tie to the MD&A total: $774 million + ~$1.4 billion ≈ **$2.2 billion** of gross fiscal 2024 provisions.
- Net fiscal 2024 charge to cost of revenue after the release: approximately **$1.7 billion** ($2.2 billion less $540 million). This is a derived figure, not a line item in the filing.
- The release is presented as a single combined number; the filing does **not** disaggregate the $540 million between inventory sold out of reserve and settlements of excess purchase obligations.

### Supporting context (not dollar charges)

- **PwC critical audit matter** (Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm, p.49): "Valuation of Inventories – Provisions for Excess or Obsolete Inventories and Excess Product Purchase Commitments" was the sole critical audit matter, citing significant management judgment in developing provisions based on inventory levels and future purchase commitments versus assumptions about future demand and market conditions. Auditor: PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP (San Jose, CA; report dated February 21, 2024).
- **Accounting policy** (Note 1, p.58): cost of sales provisions write inventory down to the lower of cost or net realizable value; once written off/down, inventory establishes a new cost basis that is not subsequently written up; a liability is recorded for non-cancelable purchase commitments for quantities in excess of future demand forecasts.

### Excluded per your instructions

- Year-end balances: total inventories $5,282 million; excess inventory purchase obligations liability $1,655 million; outstanding inventory purchase and long-term supply/capacity obligations $16.1 billion (Note 10 p.70; Note 13 p.72); prepaid supply and capacity agreements.
- Gross margin percentage impacts (the 2.7% unfavorable net effect for FY2024) and the fiscal 2023 comparatives ($1.0 billion inventory provision, $1.1 billion purchase-obligation expense, $137 million release, $2.2 billion total, 7.5% impact).

**The $14.4 billion Groq goodwill in detail:**
- In December 2025, NVIDIA entered a **non-exclusive license agreement with Groq, Inc. for its language processing unit (LPU) technology and hired certain Groq employees**; no customer contracts, existing products, or equity interests were purchased.
- Goodwill is **primarily attributable to the acquired workforce and the future development of the licensed technology**, and was recorded in the **Compute & Networking** reporting unit.
- The goodwill is **tax deductible**.
- It was recorded alongside a **$2.5 billion developed technology intangible asset** valued using a **cost-to-recreate methodology** with a five-year useful life.
- Total consideration: **$13.0 billion paid at closing** plus **$4 billion (inclusive of imputed interest) payable within one year**, recorded in Accrued and Other Current Liabilities (cash flow statement shows a $13,000M "Groq, Inc." investing outflow, p. 55).
- Pro forma results were not presented because the effect was not material.

**Note on the residual:** Balance-sheet goodwill rose $15,644M (from $5,188M to $20,832M), so roughly $1.2 billion of the $15.6 billion increase came from acquisition activity other than Groq (the 10-K separately discloses a December 15, 2025 acquisition for which NVIDIA issued 174,676 shares worth ~$31 million to a key employee, p. 34, and $1,535M of "Acquisitions, net of cash acquired" in investing cash flow, p. 55). The filing does not break out a separate goodwill amount for these other acquisitions or provide a goodwill rollforward table.

### Excluded (per your instruction) — balances at January 26, 2025
$5.2 billion total goodwill ($5,188M), consisting of **$4.8 billion** in Compute & Networking and **$370 million** in Graphics.

### Related item (not goodwill, for context)
Net intangible assets rose to **$3,306M** at January 25, 2026 from $807M, driven by acquisition-related intangibles ($3,076M net) including the Groq developed-technology asset; fiscal 2026 intangible amortization was $488M.

## Pfizer's Haleon Ownership Percentages in the 2024 Form 10-K

The filing (PFE_2024_10K.pdf, filed February 27, 2025) discloses Pfizer's Haleon plc ownership at four points in time:

| Ownership | Point in time | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **32%** | As of December 31, 2023 | Note 2C, Equity-Method Investments (doc p. 75, printed p. 66) |
| **Approximately 23%** | After the March 2024 share sale (reached during 2024, reflected in Q3 2024) | Footnote to Haleon carrying-value rollforward, Note 2C (doc p. 75) |
| **Approximately 15%** | As of December 31, 2024, after the October 2024 share sale | Note 2C (doc p. 75) and MD&A – Capital Resources (doc p. 56, printed p. 47) |
| **Approximately 7%** | First quarter of 2025 (subsequent to the balance-sheet date) | MD&A – Capital Resources (doc p. 56) |

### Supporting detail

**32% → March 2024 sale.** Pfizer "owned 32% of Haleon as of December 31, 2023." In March 2024 it sold approximately 30% of its investment (791 million ordinary shares in a global public offering plus 102 million ordinary shares sold directly to Haleon) for $3.5 billion.

**~23%.** This interim level is disclosed only in a footnote to the carrying-value rollforward, which explains a $46 million increase "for the impact of the reduction in Pfizer's ownership from approximately 32% to approximately 23% as applied to dividends with a record date in the first quarter of 2024, which were recognized in Haleon's second quarter 2024 financial statements."

**October 2024 sale → ~15%.** Pfizer sold approximately 34% of its *remaining* interest (640 million ordinary shares in a global public offering plus 61 million ordinary shares sold directly to Haleon) for $3.5 billion. Total 2024 gains on the two sales were $945 million. "After the October 2024 share sale, we owned approximately 15% of the outstanding voting shares of Haleon as of December 31, 2024." Because significant influence and board representation were lost, Pfizer discontinued the equity method and began carrying the investment as an equity security at fair value in Q4 2024 (ending equity-method carrying value: $0, reclassified to Short-term investments).

**~7% in Q1 2025.** MD&A adds: "In the first quarter of 2025, we sold an additional portion of our investment in Haleon for $3.0 billion further reducing our ownership interest to approximately 7%." Pfizer also stated it intended to monetize its remaining Haleon investment during 2025.

### One related but distinct figure
Note 2C also references a **32%** pro rata equity interest in the Consumer Healthcare JV in connection with Pfizer's indemnity of GSK's guarantee of the JV's $8.75 billion (plus €2.35 billion and £700 million) senior notes issued in March 2022 (doc p. 76, printed p. 67) — this relates to the JV, not Haleon plc directly.

I reviewed the full MD&A and related notes of Walmart's fiscal 2024 Form 10-K (WMT_2024_10K.pdf). Here are the fiscal 2024 results the company attributes, at least in part, to lapping fiscal 2023 charges or markdowns.

## Results that benefited from lapping

| Fiscal 2024 result | Lapped fiscal 2023 item | Where stated |
|---|---|---|
| **Consolidated gross profit rate** (up 27 bps to 23.7%) | Lapping "higher markdowns incurred in the prior year" (driven by the Walmart U.S. segment, alongside price management) | p. 38 (Margin) and p. 41 (Consolidated Results) |
| **Walmart U.S. gross profit rate** (up 20 bps) | Lapping "higher net markdowns incurred in the prior year" | p. 42 (Walmart U.S. Segment) |
| **Sam's Club gross profit rate** (up 55 bps) | Lapping "elevated markdowns in the prior year" | p. 44 (Sam's Club Segment) |
| **Consolidated operating expenses as a % of net sales** (down 60 bps to 20.4%) | Lapping charges of **$3.3 billion for opioid-related legal settlements** and **$0.8 billion for reorganization and restructuring of certain businesses in the Walmart International segment** | p. 38 (Margin) and p. 41 (Consolidated Results) |
| **Walmart International operating expenses as a % of segment net sales** (down 152 bps) | Lapping "business reorganization and restructuring charges incurred related to Flipkart and Massmart in fiscal 2023" | p. 43 (Walmart International Segment) |
| **Return on Investment (ROI)** (up to 15.0% from 12.7%) | Lapping "charges associated with opioid-related legal settlements as well as reorganization and restructuring expenses, all recorded in fiscal 2023" | p. 38 (Returns) |

## Notes and boundaries

- The $0.8 billion International charge appears twice under two framings: the consolidated operating-expense discussion quantifies it at $0.8 billion, while the International segment discussion names the same lapped item as the Flipkart- and Massmart-related business reorganization and restructuring charges.
- The same two charges ($3.3B opioid, $0.8B International restructuring) drive the ROI improvement, so ROI and consolidated operating-expense ratio are separate results sharing the same lapped items.
- Related but not separately counted: consolidated **operating income margin** (up 83 bps) is stated to have moved "due to the factors described above," so it is a consequence of the same drivers rather than a distinct lapping attribution.
- Excluded: **ROA** (up to 6.6% from 4.6%) — attributed to higher consolidated net income from higher operating income, with no lapping reference. Also excluded: the fiscal 2023 "lapping of the net proceeds received from the divestitures of our operations in the U.K. and Japan" in net cash used in investing activities (p. 45), which is a fiscal 2023 statement, not a fiscal 2024 benefit.
- Sam's Club's fiscal 2024 operating-expense ratio increase (46 bps) is attributed to lower fuel sales and elevated technology spend, not to lapping.

## Long-Term Debt Repayments Reported for Fiscal 2025

Walmart's fiscal 2025 Form 10-K (year ended January 31, 2025) reports long-term debt repayment amounts in two places, which differ:

### 1. Note 6 (Debt Note) — "Maturities" table: total repayment of matured debt = **$3,373 million**

The filing describes this as "significant long-term debt repayments during fiscal 2025," itemized as:

| Maturity Date | Principal Amount | Fixed vs. Floating | Interest Rate | Repayment ($M) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| April 22, 2024 | $1,500 | Fixed | 3.300% | $1,500 |
| July 8, 2024 | $990 | Fixed | 2.850% | $990 |
| July 18, 2024 | ¥40,000 | Fixed | 0.298% | $253 |
| December 15, 2024 | $630 | Fixed | 2.650% | $630 |
| **Total repayment of matured debt** | | | | **$3,373** |

- The $1,500, $990, and $630 amounts are U.S. dollar-denominated senior unsecured notes repaid at maturity.
- The $253 million is the U.S. dollar equivalent of a ¥40,000 million yen-denominated note that matured July 18, 2024.

### 2. Cash flow statement and MD&A — Repayments of long-term debt = **$3,468 million**

- **Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows** (financing activities, fiscal 2025): "Repayments of long-term debt (3,468)".
- **MD&A, Liquidity and Capital Resources — "Long-term Debt"** table (changes in long-term debt for fiscal 2025): "Repayments of long-term debt" of $(3,468) in total, all of it recorded in "Long-term debt due within one year" ($3,468), with $0 in the long-term debt column.

### Note on the two figures
The filing does not explicitly reconcile them, but the $95 million difference reflects the scope of each disclosure: Note 6's $3,373 million captures only the **significant** repayments of matured debt listed above, while the $3,468 million is the **total** long-term debt repayment reflected in financing cash flows (and in the MD&A long-term debt rollforward). Relatedly, the MD&A states that total outstanding long-term debt decreased $3.6 billion during fiscal 2025, "primarily due to maturities of certain long-term debt," and the Company had **no long-term debt issuances in fiscal 2025**.

### Excluded per your instructions
- Short-term borrowings (net change of $2,212 million in the cash flow statement; $3,068 million balance at January 31, 2025)
- Reclassifications ($2,625 million) and currency/other adjustments ($112 million) in the long-term debt rollforward
- Fiscal 2024 amounts ($4,030 million of matured debt in Note 6; $4,217 million of repayments in the fiscal 2024 cash flow statement) and fiscal 2023 amounts

**Sources:** WMT_2025_10K.pdf, Note 6 (pp. 68–69), Item 7 MD&A "Long-term Debt" (p. 44), Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows (p. 57).

## Walmart FY2026 Form 10-K (WMT_2026_10K.pdf) — cross-currency swaps as of January 31, 2026

### Amounts given in the filing

| Amount (as stated) | What it represents | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **$6,020 million** ($6.0 billion) | Notional amount of the "receive fixed-rate, pay fixed-rate cross-currency swaps designated as cash flow hedges" | Note 7, Fair Value Measurements (p. 69) |
| **$(920) million** — a net liability of $920 million | Fair value of those same cross-currency swaps (measured using the income approach with Level 2 inputs, i.e., relevant interest rate and foreign currency forward curves); primarily classified within "deferred income taxes and other" on the Consolidated Balance Sheets | Note 7 (p. 69) |
| **$0.9 billion** | The aggregate fair value of the currency swaps stated as being in a liability position as of January 31, 2026 (the rounded Item 7A version of the $920 million above) | Item 7A, Foreign Currency Risk (p. 47) |
| **$0.7 billion** | Hypothetical change in the value of the swaps from a uniform 10% weakening of the U.S. dollar against the other currencies underlying the swaps (as of January 31, 2026 market rates) | Item 7A (p. 47) |
| **$0.1 billion** | Hypothetical change in the value of the swaps from a 10% change in the interest rates underlying the swaps (as of January 31, 2026 market rates) | Item 7A (p. 47) |

### What the swaps are used for (Note 1, Cash Flow Hedges, p. 61)
- Walmart is a party to **receive fixed-rate, pay fixed-rate cross-currency interest rate swaps** used to **hedge the currency exposure associated with the forecasted payments of principal and interest of certain non-U.S. denominated debt** (the euro-, sterling- and yen-denominated long-term debt).
- Changes in the swaps' fair value are recorded in **accumulated other comprehensive loss** and subsequently reclassified into earnings in the period the hedged forecasted transaction affects earnings.
- These derivatives **mature on dates ranging from April 2026 to January 2039**.
- They are separate from the **immaterial foreign currency forward contracts** Walmart enters into in certain countries to hedge purchase commitments in non-functional currencies.

### Excluded per your instructions

Refining margins are "largely driven by differences in commodity prices" — the spread between what a refinery pays for raw materials and the market price of products produced. The dominant driver of the increase is Pfizer's November 13, 2025 acquisition of Metsera, a clinical-stage company in obesity and cardiometabolic disease. ## The offsets

**Transfers to developed technology rights.** When an IPR&D program receives regulatory approval in a major market (typically the U.S. or EU), Pfizer reclassifies the asset out of IPR&D and begins amortizing it. In 2025, $600 million for Padcev and $590 million for talazoparib (Talzenna) were transferred into developed technology rights. **Impairments.** Pfizer recorded $4,940 million of total "Certain asset impairments" in Other (income)/deductions—net for 2025 (up from $3,295 million in 2024 — a $1.6 billion increase that MD&A cites as a driver of the unfavorable swing in that line). The valuation approach is a discounted cash flow (multi-period excess earnings) method, with the key assumptions being the amount and timing of projected net cash flows (including the expected impact of competitive, legal and/or regulatory forces on the product), assumptions about the probability of technical and regulatory success (PTRS) of ongoing clinical trials, the discount rate, and the tax rate. ## Boeing's 2025 Form 10-K: Stated Purposes and Anticipated Benefits of the Spirit AeroSystems Acquisition

Boeing states the purposes and anticipated benefits of the Spirit Acquisition in three principal places: **Note 2 – Spirit Acquisition**, the **MD&A Overview**, and **Item 1A. Risk Factors**.

### 1. The core stated purpose (Note 2)

The primary purpose is stated in a single sentence: *"The Spirit Acquisition enables Boeing and Spirit to align our commercial production systems, including our Safety and Quality Management Systems, and our workforces to the same priorities, incentives and outcomes."*

This breaks into three elements Boeing emphasizes repeatedly:
- **Alignment of commercial production systems** — integrating the physical production of Boeing's own major structures rather than sourcing them from a third party.
- **Alignment of Safety and Quality Management Systems** — the explicit quality/safety rationale, tied to the FAA's post-737-9-door-plug investigation of the 737 quality control system *"including Spirit AeroSystems Holdings, Inc. (Spirit)"* and the resulting increased FAA oversight of Boeing's production, quality and safety management systems. Under that oversight, the 737 program may increase production rates or add new production lines only with FAA concurrence.
- **Alignment of workforces** to the same priorities, incentives and outcomes (Spirit brought ~15,000 employees, including Belfast operations).

### 2. Anticipated synergies, concentrated in Commercial Airplanes (Note 2)

Boeing's purchase price allocation assigns **$9,997 million of provisional goodwill to the BCA segment** with the explicit rationale: *"as we expect the majority of synergies from the Spirit Acquisition to relate to the commercial airplane segment."* This is the clearest statement of where Boeing expects the benefits to land. Related supporting items in the allocation include $2,419 million of property, plant and equipment, $1,438 million of inventories, $109 million of acquired intangibles (customer relationships, five-year weighted-average life), and $1,065 million of off-market customer contract liabilities whose amortization is expected to add revenue of $113M (2026), $133M (2027), $129M (2028), $102M (2029) and $97M (2030).

### 3. Scope of assets acquired (MD&A Overview)

Boeing describes what was obtained as an indicator of strategic purpose: all of Spirit's **Boeing-related commercial operations, including fuselages for the 737, P-8 and KC-46 Tanker programs, as well as major structures for the 767, 777 and 787 programs**, plus **Spirit's defense and aftermarket businesses** and **portions of Spirit's operations in Belfast, Ireland**. The acquisition therefore extends vertical integration across Boeing's commercial narrowbody and widebody lines, the P-8 and KC-46 tanker programs, and adds aftermarket and defense content.

### 4. Safety/quality improvement and production-rate rationale (Risk Factors)

The risk factors confirm the expected benefits and their limits. Boeing states that *"difficulties in integrating Spirit may result in the failure to realize anticipated benefits of the acquisition (including anticipated synergies and safety and quality improvements) in the expected timeframe or at all."* So the 10-K names two anticipated benefit categories explicitly: **synergies** and **safety and quality improvements**. The risk-factor discussion ties the acquisition to Boeing's broader plan to *"improve quality and safety and to address the issues identified"* by the FAA, to *"reduc[e] traveled work in our factory, as well as at our suppliers,"* and to the associated plan to *"increase the 737 production rate to 47 per month in 2026"* — i.e., the acquisition is a means of achieving rate increases and supply-chain/quality remediation at the supplier level. Boeing also notes it continues to seek opportunities *"to reduce the costs of building our aircraft, including working with our suppliers to reduce supplier costs, identifying and implementing productivity improvements."*

### 5. Financial and transaction context supporting the strategic rationale

- **Total consideration: $8,371 million**, comprising $4,704M Boeing common stock, $2,571M settlement of loans/advances/other payments to Spirit, $948M debt repaid on Spirit's behalf, $109M premium on assumed Spirit Exchangeable Notes, and $39M exchange of Spirit share-based awards (117.5M Spirit shares → 22.98M Boeing shares at a 0.1955 exchange ratio).
- **Pre-closing funding:** *"Since 2023, Boeing has provided funding in the form of loans and advance payments to Spirit to support its liquidity, rate readiness, and 787 tooling and capital expenditures."* Boeing also funded the portion of Spirit's payment to Airbus SE that Spirit could not satisfy with cash on hand at closing (concurrent with the Spirit Acquisition). ## Boeing's 2024 Form 10-K (BA_2024_10K.pdf) — causes given for lower 2024 commercial airplane deliveries

**Context:** BCA deliveries fell to **348 in 2024 from 528 in 2023** (737: 265 vs. 396; 767: 18 vs. 32; 777: 14 vs. 26; 787: 51 vs. 73; 747: 0 vs. 1) (p. 35). Notably, the filing does **not** attribute this to weak demand — it states Boeing was "experiencing strong demand from our airline customers globally" (p. 27) and BCA backlog was ~$435.2B (p. 36).

### Causes the filing explicitly links to deliveries (6)

**1. The January 5, 2024 Alaska Airlines 737-9 door-plug accident and the FAA's resulting actions.** The FAA grounded and required inspections of the ~220 in-service 737-9s, investigated Boeing's and Spirit's quality control systems, and increased oversight of production and safety management. Most directly tied to deliveries: "All 737-9 aircraft in production are undergoing this same enhanced inspection process prior to delivery" (p. 26). Boeing also slowed production rates and delayed planned rate increases, and the FAA said it would not approve 737 rate increases beyond 38/month or new lines until quality/safety compliance was achieved (pp. 26, 37, 52). Boeing also recorded $443M of 737-9 customer considerations tied to the grounding (p. 35).

**2. The IAM 751 work stoppage (Sept. 13 – Nov. 4, 2024).** The strike paused production of 737, 767, 777 and 777X aircraft and of commercial-derivative defense aircraft (KC-46A, P-8A); production resumed in December 2024. The filing states plainly: "The IAM 751 work stoppage significantly reduced aircraft deliveries in the second half of 2024" (p. 26); it is also listed among the 737 program factors adversely affecting 2024 results (p. 38).

**3. Supply chain disruptions, constraints and supplier quality issues.** "We and our suppliers are experiencing supply chain disruptions as a result of production quality issues, global supply chain constraints, and labor instability… These factors have reduced overall productivity" (p. 27). Program-level: the 767 line saw "factory disruption, including supply chain delays and quality issues"; 787 production was slowed "due to supply chain constraints as well as other production issues"; the 777X ramp was slowed "to address production challenges" (pp. 38–39). Boeing also ties the supply chain and labor instability to when "deliveries ramp up" (p. 28).

**4. 787 business class seat delays.** "Delays associated with business class seats adversely impacted 2024 deliveries and will continue to impact deliveries in 2025" (p. 39). 787 deliveries fell 73 → 51.

**5. Certification and entry-into-service delays on new models (737-7/-10 and 777X).** 737-7/-10 certification was delayed (including the engine anti-ice engineering solution), leaving ~35 737-7/-10 aircraft in inventory at year-end 2024 (p. 38). For the 777X, flight test delays and revised certification timelines pushed first delivery of the 777-9 to 2026, the 777-8 Freighter to 2028, and the 777-8 passenger aircraft to no earlier than 2030, and the ramp slowdown "resulted in higher production costs and further customer delivery delays" (p. 39).

**6. U.S.–China trade/geopolitical conditions.** The filing warns that if Boeing cannot "deliver aircraft to customers in China consistent with our assumptions… we may experience reduced deliveries and/or lower market share" (p. 13). ~40 737-8 aircraft built for Chinese customers sat in inventory at year-end 2024, expected to be delivered in 2025 (p. 38).

### Excluded per your instruction (costs, rates, revenue only — not linked to delivery volume)
- **777X and 767 reach-forward losses** ($4,079M) — a loss/cost item, and the "new IAM 751 agreement" pay increases and non-union pay enhancements (cost/margin pressure only).
- **The FAA 38-per-month rate cap** as such — the filing states this as a production-rate approval matter; the delivery linkage comes from the enhanced inspection of production 737-9 aircraft, not the rate cap.
- **737 MAX customer concessions ($0.9B paid) and "lower customer delivery payments"** — these affect the *price* of deliveries, not the number of deliveries.

- **A minor item:** the 747 — the last aircraft was delivered in February 2023 after production ended in Q4 2022, accounting for the 1-aircraft difference (p. 37).
